searchDocs.content: </> bootstrap.bootstrap() → () Writes every maze singleton. Call once, before startup.

searchDocs.title: DEFAULT_FRAME_MS​
searchDocs.content: </> budget.DEFAULT_FRAME_MS: number Milliseconds per frame the whole maze pipeline may spend. Four is the smallest allowance that still drains a chunk's walls within a frame or two of the chunk arriving, which is what keeps the build backlog at zero for a walking player. Smaller is counterproductive rather than merely slower: whatever does not fit carries over, and every stage then repays its per-frame setup against a backlog that never clears. Larger buys throughput only a teleporting player could use, at the cost of pushing the server frame past the 16.6ms a 60Hz tick allows.

searchDocs.title: defaults​
searchDocs.content: </> budget.defaults() → MazeConfig-- A fresh config table. The starting configuration, written to the singleton by bootstrap. The four radii start at zero because they are outputs — the observers system derives them from viewDistanceCells on its first pass.

searchDocs.title: deadlineFrom​

searchDocs.title: build​
searchDocs.content: </> build.build(world: jecs.World) → ( () → (),-- Update function. () → ()-- Cleanup function. ) Advances every in-flight build job. Runs in Phases.Update, ahead of load. Finishing work already started outranks starting more. A half-built chunk is already paying for its residency without being useful, so the frame's allowance goes to completing it before any new chunk is generated. Unlike the other maze systems this ignores resyncNeeded — a build backlog has to keep draining whether or not anyone is moving.

searchDocs.title: client
searchDocs.content: client This item only works when running on the client. Clientcore Client entry point. Starts replication, boots the ECS, mounts the UI, then pulls the initial world snapshot from the server. The listeners go on before lync.start, which seals what a side has attached; start then waits for the server's remotes to replicate, so everything below it runs on a live connection. startup is handed the shared systems alone. Applying replication is the only thing the client ever did on a tick, and Lync dispatches that to the listeners below instead, so there are no client-only systems to register.

searchDocs.title: client/replicator
searchDocs.content: client/replicator This item only works when running on the client. Clientclient-system The client half of the shared replecs replicator.

searchDocs.title: step​
searchDocs.content: </> builder.step( world: jecs.World, playerChunks: {{ x: number, y: number }},-- Observer positions in chunk space. deadline: number-- os.clock() value to stop at. ) → () Spends the frame's remaining budget across every live job. Walls come first across all jobs, then prefab detail across all jobs. A chunk with bare walls is navigable; a chunk with props and no walls is a player falling through the world, so walls win the budget every time. Prefabs are only queued here. The clone system copies them node by node and a placement lands in the world from its own completion callback some frames later — which is also why the queue must be drained by that separate system and not from here, since this function returns early once no jobs remain. Jobs whose chunk has already been detached are dropped up front, before any budget is spent. The loops below consume from the end of the list, so a dead job sitting earlier would survive every frame the budget ran out on — one was observed lingering for seconds after its chunk unloaded. Always builds at least one thing per call, so an exhausted budget slows the world filling in rather than freezing it.

searchDocs.title: Signal​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Signal { Connect: ( self, callback ) → RBXScriptConnection ConnectParallel: ( self, callback ) → RBXScriptConnection Once: ( self, callback ) → RBXScriptConnection Wait: (self) → T... } The subset of RBXScriptSignal this module needs, so it also accepts custom signal implementations.

searchDocs.title: collect​
searchDocs.content: </> collect.collect(signal: Signal<T...>) → ( () → any,-- Drains one firing per call, returning its arguments; nothing when empty. RBXScriptConnection -- Disconnect this when the consumer goes away. ) Buffers a signal's firings for later draining. Arguments are stored flattened in one array rather than as a table per event, with a parallel array of argument counts to slice them back apart. Events fire far more often than they are drained, so this avoids allocating a table per firing. When the buffer empties, both cursors reset to the start so the arrays do not grow without bound. The caller owns the returned connection and must disconnect it, normally in the system's cleanup function. local nextPlayer, connection = collect(Players.PlayerAdded) -- inside the system: for player in nextPlayer do -- one iteration per firing since the last tick end

searchDocs.content: </> demolish.demolish(world: jecs.World) → ( () → (),-- Update function. () → ()-- Cleanup function. ) Destroys queued chunk contents until the frame's shared deadline. Runs inPhases.PreUpdate, alongside hide — teardown gets first claim on the frame because it is what makes the next frame cheaper. Runs unconditionally rather than behind resyncNeeded: a teardown backlog has to keep draining whether or not anyone is moving.

searchDocs.content: </> type Placement = mazeTypes.Placement Re-exported from mazeTypes so the generation passes can name it without requiring this module, and so every existing components.Placement keeps resolving. See mazeTypes for why it lives there.

searchDocs.title: MazeFrame​
searchDocs.content: </> interface MazeFrame { deadline: number-- os.clock() value every stage stops at. } This frame's shared allowance, stamped once by the frame system. Every budgeted stage stops at the same instant, so the pipeline as a whole cannot exceed frameMs no matter how the work is distributed. Stages that run late in the phase order get whatever earlier stages left, which is what makes phase order the priority order.

searchDocs.title: MazeStreaming​
searchDocs.content: </> interface MazeStreaming { positions: {MazePosition}-- One entry per observer, in world-cell space. chunkFrames: {MazePosition}-- The same observers snapped to chunk coordinates. blockFrames: {MazePosition}-- Scratch buffer reused per chunk for detail-block distance. signature: string?-- Detail-block fingerprint of the last processed frame. resyncNeeded: boolean-- Observers moved far enough to warrant a streaming pass. loadsOutstanding: boolean-- The load system ran out of budget with work left. promotionsDeferred: boolean-- The detail system hit its in-flight job cap. } Everything the streaming pipeline needs to know about where players are. Each field has exactly one writer: observers writes the positions, frames, signature and resyncNeeded; load writes loadsOutstanding; detail writes promotionsDeferred. Keep it that way — the single-writer rule is what stops this becoming a hidden global again.

searchDocs.title: BuildAssets​

searchDocs.title: PrefabCache​
searchDocs.content: </> interface PrefabCache { partCounts: {[Instance ]: number}-- Memoized BasePart count per prefab. warnedMissing: {[string]: boolean}-- "folder/name" keys already warned about. } Memoization for prefab inspection, which is pure but expensive enough that recomputing it per placement shows up in a profile.

searchDocs.title: detach​
searchDocs.content: </> demolition.detach( world: jecs.World, chunkEntity: Entity ) → () Detaches a chunk's instances and queues them for piecewise destruction. Detaching first is load-bearing: letting the subtree linger in Workspace while a slow destroy queue drains measured mean 31.54ms against 12.48ms.

searchDocs.title: drain​
searchDocs.content: </> demolition.drain( world: jecs.World, deadline: number-- os.clock() value to stop at. ) → () Destroys queued chunk contents until the frame's shared deadline. Walks a folder one child at a time rather than calling Destroy on the root: destroying a whole chunk atomically is the single largest hitch the pipeline can produce. Nested folders are pushed onto the queue rather than recursed into, so the walk stays interruptible at any depth. Always destroys at least one thing per call, so a blown budget slows the queue instead of stalling it.

searchDocs.title: Candidate​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Candidate { key: number-- Detail block key. bucket: {Placement}-- The block's prefabs. distance: number-- Chebyshev distance to the nearest observer, in blocks. } A detail block that wants promoting.

searchDocs.title: MAX_PENDING_DETAIL_JOBS​
searchDocs.content: </> detail.MAX_PENDING_DETAIL_JOBS: number How many prefab build jobs may be in flight at once. Queueing more than the build budget can drain just spreads every block's completion out instead of finishing the nearest ones first.

searchDocs.title: detail​
searchDocs.content: </> detail.detail(world: jecs.World) → ( () → (),-- Update function. () → ()-- Cleanup function. ) Runs detail-block streaming across every loaded chunk. Runs inPhases.PostUpdate, after load has had its chance to add chunks. Writes MazeStreaming.promotionsDeferred — the only field this system owns — so observers keeps requesting resyncs while blocks are still waiting on the job cap.

searchDocs.title: flush​
searchDocs.content: </> flush.flush( _world: jecs.World-- Injected by planck; unused here. ) → ( () → (),-- Update function. () → ()-- Cleanup function. ) Flushes the maze namespace. Runs in Phases.Last. Lync buffers every fire and every request until a flush, so without this nothing leaves either side. Phases.Last is what makes it the tick's final word: replecs fires in the default Phases.Update, and a flush connected to PostSimulation by hand would race that on connection order instead. No budget is passed. The budget throttles replicated sets, and this namespace has none — packets and requests always go out whole.

searchDocs.title: CELL_TYPE_BY_MASK​
searchDocs.content: </> features.CELL_TYPE_BY_MASK: {CellType} Cell topology for each of the 16 wall combinations, indexed bymask + 1 where the mask is up=1, down=2, left=4, right=8.

searchDocs.title: CELL_ROTATION_BY_MASK​
searchDocs.content: </> features.CELL_ROTATION_BY_MASK: {number} Degrees each wall combination is rotated from its canonical topology, so a prop authored for one dead end fits all four.

searchDocs.title: place​
searchDocs.content: </> features.place( maze: Maze, random: Random ,-- Seeded per chunk. out: {Placement}-- Appended to, one entry per placed feature. ) → {Placement}-- The same table, for chaining. Runs the feature pass over a chunk. Every feature gets one guaranteed attempt first, then the list is rolled repeatedly until features cover FEATURE_OCCUPANCY_CAP of the chunk, the free cells run out, or too many passes in a row place nothing. Must run after maze.carve — cells are classified by their finished walls.

searchDocs.title: chunk​
searchDocs.content: </> generate.chunk( worldSeed: number,-- Seed every chunk derives from. chunkX: number,-- Chunk column. chunkY: number-- Chunk row. ) → ( Maze,-- The finished maze, walls materialised. {Placement},-- Rooms and features to build. {mesher.Run}-- Merged wall runs to build. ) Generates one chunk from its coordinates alone. The pass order is load-bearing: rooms.place stamps footprints and marks their cells captured. maze.carve carves corridors, routing around anything captured. maze.openDoors opens the chunk-border doorways. features.place classifies the finished corridors and drops props in. grid.materialiseWalls freezes the edge grids onto the cell records. Everything is derived from the chunk seed, so the same coordinates always produce the same chunk regardless of what order chunks load in.

searchDocs.title: stripOwnedBorders​
searchDocs.content: </> generate.stripOwnedBorders( runs: {mesher.Run}-- Mutated in place. ) → {mesher.Run}-- The same table, foreign borders removed. Drops the wall runs that belong to the neighbouring chunk. Every chunk meshes all four of its borders, so each shared border would be built twice — once by each side. By convention a chunk owns its far borders and the neighbour owns the near ones, so the runs on x == 0 and y == 0 are discarded here.

searchDocs.title: MazePosition​
searchDocs.content: </> interface MazePosition { x: number-- Cell column. y: number-- Cell row. } A position measured in maze cells.

searchDocs.title: getCenterPosition​
searchDocs.content: </> geometry.getCenterPosition( x: number,-- Cell column. y: number,-- Cell row. cellSize: number-- Studs per cell. ) → Vector3  World-space centre of a cell, at floor height.

searchDocs.title: cframeToMazePosition​
searchDocs.content: </> geometry.cframeToMazePosition(cframe: CFrame ) → MazePosition The cell a world-space CFrame falls in. The inverse of [geometry.getCenterPosition]: cell x spans world X from -(x + 1) * MAZE_CELL_SIZE up to -x * MAZE_CELL_SIZE, which is where the walls either side of it are built. Subtracting half a cell before flooring shifts those bounds by half a cell, so everything in the near half of a cell reports as its neighbour and an observer's cell is off by one for half of every cell it crosses.

searchDocs.title: nearestChebyshev​
searchDocs.content: </> geometry.nearestChebyshev( x: number,-- Column to measure from. y: number,-- Row to measure from. frames: {MazePosition}-- Points to measure to. ) → number-- Distance to the nearest frame, or math.huge if there are none. Chebyshev distance from a point to the nearest of several frames. Chebyshev rather than Euclidean because streaming works in square rings: a radius of 2 should mean the 5x5 block of chunks around the observer, corners included.

searchDocs.title: sortFarthestFirst​
searchDocs.content: </> jobs.sortFarthestFirst( list: {BuildJob},-- Sorted in place. playerChunks: {{ x: number, y: number }}-- Observer positions in chunk space. ) → () Sorts jobs farthest-observer-first. The build loop consumes jobs from the end of the list, so farthest-first ordering is what makes the nearest chunk build first. Reversing this builds the far side of the world while the player stares at a hole.

searchDocs.title: Cell​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Cell { x: number-- Cell column within the chunk, 0-indexed. y: number-- Cell row within the chunk, 0-indexed. wallUp: boolean-- Solid edge on the +Y side. wallDown: boolean-- Solid edge on the -Y side. wallLeft: boolean-- Solid edge on the -X side. wallRight: boolean-- Solid edge on the +X side. claimed: boolean-- Something has been placed here; no second placement may take it. captured: boolean-- Inside a room footprint, so the carver must skip it. reserved: boolean-- Borders a room and is held clear so rooms do not abut. } One maze cell. The three flags are live throughout generation. The four wall booleans arenot: they stay false until grid.materialiseWalls copies them down from the edge grids once carving has finished. Read walls off the edge grids during generation, and off the cell afterwards.

searchDocs.title: Maze​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Maze { size: number-- Cell count along each axis. cells: {{Cell}}-- Cell records, indexed cells[y][x], both 0-indexed. horizontal: {{boolean}}-- Edges perpendicular to Y, indexed horizontal[y][x], y in 0..size. vertical: {{boolean}}-- Edges perpendicular to X, indexed vertical[y][x], x in 0..size. } One chunk's maze. Walls live on the edges between cells, not on the cells themselves, because an edge is shared: cells[y][x].wallUp and cells[y + 1][x].wallDown are the same wall. Storing it once on horizontal/vertical means a carve can never leave the two sides disagreeing.

searchDocs.title: materialiseWalls​
searchDocs.content: </> grid.materialiseWalls(maze: Maze) → () Copies the edge grids down onto every cell's four wall booleans. Call this once, after all carving and placement has finished. The cell wall fields are a read-only view for consumers; anything that still needs to change a wall must go through grid.setSide before this runs.

searchDocs.title: load​
searchDocs.content: </> load.load(world: jecs.World) → ( () → (),-- Update function. () → ()-- Cleanup function. ) Generates as many nearby chunks as the frame has left. Runs inPhases.PostUpdate, last of the stages that spend the budget. Generating a chunk is a single indivisible ~5ms unit, larger than the whole frame allowance, so this stage always overruns when it runs at all. That is tolerable only because it runs after build: the deadline is re-stamped every frame, so an overrun here costs the tail of this frame rather than starving the incremental stages, which get a fresh allowance next tick. It still forces one chunk through per pass. Dropping that guarantee was tried and is much worse — under sustained traversal load never won a frame at all and the world failed to rebuild, ending a 12-hop run with an empty maze and 72.8% stalls. Writes MazeStreaming.loadsOutstanding — the only field this system owns — so observers keeps requesting resyncs until the backlog clears. Deliberately not gated on resyncNeeded. That flag is edge-triggered on the observers' detail-block signature changing, but chunks can go missing for reasons that have nothing to do with anyone moving — an unload, a teardown, a momentary gap in observer tracking. Gating on it stalled the pipeline for good: destroy a chunk inside the load radius while the player stands still and nothing ever regenerated it, because a stationary player's signature never changes again. Since the world then stops growing, and streaming leaves the client with no ground, that also read as the character being unable to move. Detecting the gap is cheap enough to do unconditionally — a handful of table lookups over the chunks in radius. Only registry.ensure is expensive, and that only runs when something is genuinely missing.

searchDocs.title: carve​
searchDocs.content: </> maze.carve( maze: Maze,-- A maze whose edges have been filled solid. random: Random ,-- Seeded per chunk, so carving is deterministic. bias: number?-- Newest-cell bias in 0..1. Defaults to 0.75. ) → () Carves a perfect maze into maze, opening edges as it goes. Cells already marked captured — room footprints and their approaches — are left alone. bias selects between depth-first and Prim-like behaviour: at 1 the walk always extends the newest cell, giving long winding corridors; at 0 it picks a random frontier cell, giving a bushier maze with more junctions.

searchDocs.title: MazeConfig​
searchDocs.content: </> interface MazeConfig { viewDistanceCells: number-- Requested detail view distance in cells. detailRadius: number-- Detail blocks kept loaded around an observer. detailDropRadius: number-- Distance at which detail blocks are cached out. loadRadius: number-- Chunks generated around an observer. unloadRadius: number-- Distance at which chunks are destroyed. frameMs: number-- Total milliseconds per frame the whole maze pipeline may spend. } Streaming tuning. viewDistanceCells and frameMs are the inputs; the four radii are derived by the observers system. searchDocs.title: beginNext​
searchDocs.content: </> placement.beginNext( world: jecs.World,-- Named explicitly: this function writes components. assets: BuildAssets,-- For the prefab root. cache: PrefabCache,-- Missing-prefab warnings. job: BuildJob-- Mutated: its placement index advances. ) → () Starts the job's next placement and advances past it. Returns as soon as the clone is queued, not when it is built — the entity gains its PlacementModel and loses Processing later, from the completion callback. The job therefore moves on immediately and several placements can be in flight at once. Positioning happens on completion rather than at enqueue time becauseslowClone hands back an empty root; pivoting it before its parts exist would move nothing. The completion callback re-checks its destination. Streaming takes frames, and the chunk can be torn down in the meantime — without that check the finished model would be parented into a detached folder and leak.

A resync is requested when the observers' detail-block fingerprint changes, when the radii change, or when load or detail reported unfinished work last frame — otherwise the pipeline would stall halfway through a backlog while the player stood still.

searchDocs.title: DOOR_SIDE_SEED​
searchDocs.content: </> seed.DOOR_SIDE_SEED: {[string]: number} Per-side salt, so a chunk's east and north doorways are not drawn from the same sequence.

searchDocs.title: newWorldSeed​
searchDocs.content: </> seed.newWorldSeed() → number Draws a fresh world seed. Called once by the bootstrap system.

searchDocs.title: chunkKey​
searchDocs.content: </> seed.chunkKey( chunkX: number,-- Chunk column. chunkY: number-- Chunk row. ) → string The "x,y" key a chunk is stored under.

searchDocs.title: chunkSeed​
searchDocs.content: </> seed.chunkSeed( worldSeed: number, chunkX: number,-- Chunk column. chunkY: number-- Chunk row. ) → number-- Seed for this chunk's Random. Hashes a chunk's coordinates against the world seed. The two multipliers are large odd constants — the same ones Knuth-style integer hashes use — chosen so that adjacent chunks, whose coordinates differ by one, land far apart in the output. The final xor-shift mixes the high bits back down, otherwise nearby chunks share low-bit structure and their mazes come out visibly similar. The rotate between the two coordinate terms is load-bearing. Folding both in with a single bxor puts them at the same bit positions, where negating both coordinates cancels out and (x, y) hashes to the same value as (-x, -y) — a world point-symmetric about the origin, with 16% of chunks in a 121x121 block sharing a maze with their opposite. Rotating between the terms breaks the symmetry: the same sweep collides zero times.

searchDocs.title: doorOffsets​

The two cell offsets where a chunk border is open. Both chunks either side of a border call this with the same arguments and get the same answer, which is what lets independently generated chunks line up.

searchDocs.title: server
searchDocs.content: server This item only works when running on the server. Servercore Server entry point. Starts replication, initialises the maze singletons, answers each client's request for the initial world snapshot, then boots the ECS. The order matters twice over. bootstrap must finish before startup registers any system, because system registration order is not guaranteed and several systems read those singletons on their first tick. And the responder must be attached before lync.start, which seals what a side has attached and publishes the remotes a client is waiting on.

() → ()-- Cleanup function. ) Fires world changes to every ready player, 20 times a second. Replicating once per frame would send far more traffic than gameplay needs; 20 Hz is the rate the client interpolates against. Nothing leaves here — theflush system in Phases.Last hands the buffered fires to the engine.

searchDocs.title: show​
searchDocs.content: </> show.show(world: jecs.World) → ( () → (),-- Update function. () → ()-- Cleanup function; drops any half-streamed hierarchies. ) Parents in as many pending placements as the frame has left. Runs inPhases.Update, alongside build, acting on the intent detail set last frame. Draining runs before enqueueing: hierarchies already part-way into the world should finish before more are started, or everything sits half-assembled at once. Always reveals at least one placement per pass, even over budget, so a tight budget slows the reveal instead of stalling it forever.

searchDocs.content: </> slowClone.enqueue( template: Instance ,-- Source hierarchy. Not modified. onComplete: (Instance ) → ()-- Called with the finished root. ) → Instance -- The detached root clone. Queues a hierarchy to be copied and returns its root immediately. The returned root is detached and initially childless; it gains its contents over the following frames. onComplete fires once, deferred, when the last node has been copied.

searchDocs.title: Job​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Job { root: Instance -- The hierarchy being streamed in. chunks: {Chunk}-- Outstanding work. chunkHead: number-- Next chunk index, 1-based. onComplete: (Instance ) → ()-- Called once every descendant is back in place. } One hierarchy part-way into the world.

searchDocs.title: enqueue​
searchDocs.content: </> slowParent.enqueue( subject: Instance ,-- Detached hierarchy to admit. destination: Instance ,-- Where the root belongs. onComplete: (Instance ) → ()-- Called once streaming finishes. ) → Instance -- The same subject, now parented but not yet filled. Queues a hierarchy to be streamed into destination. The root is parented immediately, but it is emptied first, so this call admits exactly one instance no matter how large the subtree is.

searchDocs.title: processNext​
searchDocs.content: </> slowParent.processNext( deadline: number,-- os.clock() value to stop at. maxNodes: number?-- Hard cap on nodes admitted this call. Defaults to 50. ) → number-- Nodes admitted. Admits nodes until the deadline passes or the per-call cap is reached, oldest job first. The node cap exists because time is not the only cost here: a burst of parent writes inside one frame is charged by the engine on the following frame regardless of how quickly the writes themselves returned. Always admits at least one node per call, so an over-budget frame still makes progress rather than leaving hierarchies half-visible forever.

searchDocs.title: cell​
searchDocs.content: </> spawn.cell(world: jecs.World) → MazePosition-- Where to place the character, in world-cell space. Finds a spawn cell in the origin chunk, generating the nine chunks around the origin first so the player lands on solid ground with neighbours already streaming. Falls back through three tiers: a cell with clear surroundings, then any unoccupied cell, then the origin itself.

searchDocs.title: spawnPlayer​

Join and leave events are buffered through collect rather than handled in the signal callback, so entity creation happens inside the scheduler. Players already present when the system starts are tracked immediately, which matters on a hot reload.

searchDocs.title: unload​
searchDocs.content: </> unload.unload(world: jecs.World) → ( () → (),-- Update function. () → ()-- Cleanup function. ) Unloads every chunk beyond the unload radius. Runs in Phases.Last, so a chunk is never destroyed in the same frame something else was still building into it. The unload radius sits one chunk beyond the load radius, giving a band where a chunk is neither generated nor destroyed — without it, walking back and forth over a chunk boundary would rebuild the same chunk repeatedly. Stale chunks are collected before any are removed, because unloading mutates the registry table being iterated.

searchDocs.title: Position​
searchDocs.content: </> interface Position { x: number-- Column in world-cell space. y: number-- Row in world-cell space. } Somewhere an observer is standing.

searchDocs.title: positionKey​
searchDocs.content: </> wallOrder.positionKey(positions: {Position}) → string-- Empty when there are no observers. A key identifying where the observers stand, at cell resolution. Used to decide when a chunk's wall ordering has gone stale. Cell resolution rather than detail-block resolution because a block is eight cells across, and waiting that long to re-prioritise shows up as walls filling in behind the player. Sorted, so the key does not change just because the query returned two players in a different order.

searchDocs.title: sortRunsFarthestFirst​
searchDocs.content: </> wallOrder.sortRunsFarthestFirst( runs: {Run},-- Sorted in place. baseX: number,-- Chunk origin column, in world cells. baseY: number,-- Chunk origin row, in world cells. positions: {Position}-- Observer positions in world-cell space. ) → boolean-- True if the runs are now ordered. Orders wall runs farthest-observer-first, in place. Farthest first because the build loop pops the last element, so the nearest wall is the next one built. Distance is Chebyshev, matching every other radius in the streaming pipeline. Returns whether it ordered anything. With no observers there is no meaningful order, and the caller must not record a sort key it did not earn — otherwise the ordering would be skipped forever once observers appear.

searchDocs.title: CORNER_PAD​
searchDocs.content: </> walls.CORNER_PAD: number Extra length on every wall run so runs meeting at a corner overlap instead of leaving a hairline gap. The epsilon keeps the overlap just under a full thickness, so the join does not bulge.

searchDocs.title: VERTICAL_WALL_HEIGHT​
searchDocs.content: </> walls.VERTICAL_WALL_HEIGHT: number Vertical runs are a hair shorter than horizontal ones so that where the two cross, one owns the cap and they do not z-fight along the top edge.
